section_candidates.excerpt: Introduction The Waterberg Group is a thick Proterozoic sedimentary succession deposited on Archean and Paleoproterozoic rocks of the Kaapvaal Craton (Figure 1), including the ~2.06 Ga Bushveld Complex (Walraven and Hattingh, 1993; Walraven, 1997; de Waal and Armstrong, 2000; Buick et al. , 2001; Eglington and Armstrong, 2004). Rb–Sr and U–Pb dates of ~1.4 to ~1.3 Ga for the Pilanesberg Dyke Swarm and syenite of the Leeuwfontein complex that intrude parts of the group have generally been inferred to provide a younger age limit for the group (e.g. Jansen, 1982; Tankard et al., 1982; Walraven et al., 1990; Emerman, 1991). Widespread dolerite sills that intrude the Waterberg Group and predate Jurassic Karoo magmatism have common

matism in southern Africa and place tighter age constraints on the Waterberg Group than previously available. In South Africa, ~1.88 Ga dolerite intrudes upper Waterberg strata, constraining most, if not all, of the succession to have accumulated between ~2.06 Ga (age of the underlying Bushveld Complex) and ~1.88 Ga. This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Paleomagnetic data for the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma intrusions yield a new Paleoproterozoic pole for the Kaapvaal Craton, and comparisons between the ~1927 and ~1879 to ~1872 Ma post- Waterberg dolerites and broadly coeval mafic rocks elsewhere in South Africa and Zimbabwe help to constrain the nature and temporal and spatial distribution of intraplate Paleoproterozoic magmatism in the region. Stratigraphy and depositional setting of the Waterberg Group The Waterberg Group has been the subject of numerous stratigraphic and sedimentological studies in South Africa, and the following information is primarily from Jansen (1982), Callaghan et al. (1991), van der Neut et al. (1991) and Callaghan (1993). Across the Waterberg plateau and adjacent areas (Figures 2 and 3), the group has a composite stratigraphic thickness of as much as 7km. The lower part of the group there (Swaershoek, Alma and Sterkrivier Formations), and the entire succession exposed in the Middleburg area, consist dominantly of sandstones and rudites (conglomerates and sedimentary breccias) deposited in alluvial fan and fan-delta environments. These rocks accumulated at least partly in localized basins controlled by movement along the Thabazimbi–Murchison Lineament

This unit is succeeded by more widespread sandstones and conglomerates of the Mannyelanong Formation, which is the basal unit of the Waterberg Group as defined in Botswana. The Mannyelanong Formation is correlated with the Skilpadkop Formation in South Africa (Carney et al. , 1994) and forms discontinuous outcrops in southeastern Botswana that are erosional remnants of a sheet of alluvial fan and braidplain deposits derived from an upfaulted source area to the south (Key, 1983; Aldiss et al. , 1989; Williamson, 1996). Rb–Sr and U–Pb dates of ~1.4 to ~1.3 Ga for the Pilanesberg Dyke Swarm and syenite of the Leeuwfontein complex that intrude parts of the group have generally been inferred to provide a younger age limit for the group (e.g. Jansen, 1982; Tankard et al., 1982; Walraven et al., 1990; Emerman, 1991). Widespread dolerite sills that intrude the Waterberg Group and predate Jurassic Karoo magmatism have common

matism in southern Africa and place tighter age constraints on the Waterberg Group than previously available. In South Africa, ~1.88 Ga dolerite intrudes upper Waterberg strata, constraining most, if not all, of the succession to have accumulated between ~2.06 Ga (age of the underlying Bushveld Complex) and ~1.88 Ga. This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. section_candidates.excerpt: Introduction The Waterberg Group is a thick Proterozoic sedimentary succession deposited on Archean and Paleoproterozoic rocks of the Kaapvaal Craton (Figure 1), including the ~2.06 Ga Bushveld Complex (Walraven and Hattingh, 1993; Walraven, 1997; de Waal and Armstrong, 2000; Buick et al. , 2001; Eglington and Armstrong, 2004). Rb–Sr and U–Pb dates of ~1.4 to ~1.3 Ga for the Pilanesberg Dyke Swarm and syenite of the Leeuwfontein complex that intrude parts of the group have generally been inferred to provide a younger age limit for the group (e.g. Jansen, 1982; Tankard et al., 1982; Walraven et al., 1990; Emerman, 1991). Widespread dolerite sills that intrude the Waterberg Group and predate Jurassic Karoo magmatism have common

matism in southern Africa and place tighter age constraints on the Waterberg Group than previously available. In South Africa, ~1.88 Ga dolerite intrudes upper Waterberg strata, constraining most, if not all, of the succession to have accumulated between ~2.06 Ga (age of the underlying Bushveld Complex) and ~1.88 Ga. This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Older, ~1927 Ma dolerite in Botswana is similar in age and geochemistry to basalts in the craton-margin Olifantshoek Supergroup, suggesting t

This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Paleomagnetic data for the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma intrusions yield a new Paleoproterozoic pole for the Kaapvaal Craton, and comparisons between the ~1927 and ~1879 to ~1872 Ma post- Waterberg dolerites and broadly coeval mafic rocks elsewhere in South Africa and Zimbabwe help to constrain the nature and temporal and spatial distribution of intraplate Paleoproterozoic magmatism in the region. Stratigraphy and depositional setting of the Waterberg Group The Waterberg Group has been the subject of numerous stratigraphic and sedimentological studies in South Africa, and the following information is primarily from Jansen (1982), Callaghan et al. (1991), van der Neut et al. (1991) and Callaghan (1993). Across the Waterberg plateau and adjacent areas (Figures 2 and 3), the group has a composite stratigraphic thickness of as much as 7km. The lower part of the group there (Swaershoek, Alma and Sterkrivier Formations), and the entire succession exposed in the Middleburg area, consist dominantly of sandstones and rudites (conglomerates and sedimentary breccias) deposited in alluvial fan and fan-delta environments. section_candidates.excerpt: Introduction The Waterberg Group is a thick Proterozoic sedimentary succession deposited on Archean and Paleoproterozoic rocks of the Kaapvaal Craton (Figure 1), including the ~2.06 Ga Bushveld Complex (Walraven and Hattingh, 1993; Walraven, 1997; de Waal and Armstrong, 2000; Buick et al. , 2001; Eglington and Armstrong, 2004). Rb–Sr and U–Pb dates of ~1.4 to ~1.3 Ga for the Pilanesberg Dyke Swarm and syenite of the Leeuwfontein complex that intrude parts of the group have generally been inferred to provide a younger age limit for the group (e.g. Jansen, 1982; Tankard et al., 1982; Walraven et al., 1990; Emerman, 1991). Widespread dolerite sills that intrude the Waterberg Group and predate Jurassic Karoo magmatism have common

matism in southern Africa and place tighter age constraints on the Waterberg Group than previously available. In South Africa, ~1.88 Ga dolerite intrudes upper Waterberg strata, constraining most, if not all, of the succession to have accumulated between ~2.06 Ga (age of the underlying Bushveld Complex) and ~1.88 Ga. This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Older, ~1927 Ma dolerite in Botswana is similar in age and geochemistry to basalts in the craton-margin Olifantshoek Supergroup, suggesting t

terberg strata, constraining most, if not all, of the succession to have accumulated between ~2.06 Ga (age of the underlying Bushveld Complex) and ~1.88 Ga. This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Older, ~1927 Ma dolerite in Botswana is similar in age and geochemistry to basalts in the craton-margin Olifantshoek Supergroup, suggesting that the mafic magmatism in those two regions is genetically related. R.E. HANSON, W.A. GOSE, J.L. CROWLEY, J. RAMEZANI, S.A. BOWRING, D.S. BULLEN, R.P. HALL, J.A.

Paleomagnetic data for the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma intrusions yield a new Paleoproterozoic pole for the Kaapvaal Craton, and comparisons between the ~1927 and ~1879 to ~1872 Ma post- Waterberg dolerites and broadly coeval mafic rocks elsewhere in South Africa and Zimbabwe help to constrain the nature and temporal and spatial distribution of intraplate Paleoproterozoic magmatism in the region. Stratigraphy and depositional setting of the Waterberg Group The Waterberg Group has been the subject of numerous stratigraphic and sedimentological studies in South Africa, and the following information is primarily from Jansen (1982), Callaghan et al. (1991), van der Neut et al. (1991) and Callaghan (1993). Across the Waterberg plateau and adjacent areas (Figures 2 and 3), the group has a composite stratigraphic thickness of as much as 7km. The lower part of the group there (Swaershoek, Alma and Sterkrivier Formations), and the entire succession exposed in the Middleburg area, consist dominantly of sandstones and rudites (conglomerates and sedimentary breccias) deposited in alluvial fan and fan-delta environments. Detailed stepwise thermal demagnetization isolated two components. The soft compo- nent (component A) was interpreted as a remagnetization in the recent geomagnetic field. The hard component (compo- nent B) with higher unblocking-temperatures was carried by hematite. Its site-mean direction is D/I = 77.6°/-24.3° (κ = 5.4, α95 = 18.3°, N = 15 sites) before, and D/I = 72.2°/11.5° ( κ = 24.6, α95 = 7.9°) after tilt correction. It passes a fold test (Mesozoic folding) at 99% confidence level and reversal test at 95% confidence level. The corresponding pole locates at 17.3°N, 214.5°E (dp = 4.1°, dm = 8.0°). A best fit of paleo- magnetic poles from the NCB, Baltica, Siberia and the ap- parent polar wander path for Laurentia suggests a long-lived connection between these pale o-continents between ~1800 and 1350 Ma. Two absolute age values are available for the lower part of the Zolotitsa River section: 550 ±4.6 Ma and 550±5.3 Ma. These ages were determined using zircons from the volcanic rock interlayers. The rocks investigated in this study are characterized by the low anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility, by the absence of any predominant directions of the half-axes of the ellipsoids of anisotropy, and by the planar type of the latter. The main carrier of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) is hematite in all rocks, magnetite being found occasionally in gray rocks. The detailed stepwise thermal demagnetization of the samples proved the multicomponent composition of the rocks. The low- and medium-temperature components resulted from the demagnetization of the rocks during various interval of geologic time. The high-temperature component is characterized by the positive tests of folding, reversal, and correlation, hence being a primary one. Variations of its direction along the rock sequence were used in this study to identify 27 zones of direct and 28 zones of reversed polarity for the total amount of the rocks investigated in this study. The J(T ) peaks in the upper part of the rock sequence were recorded in all samples, except for those from the Vendian interval where the peaks diminish with some samples showing a reversed J(T ) curve pattern. A similar eﬀect is often observed in experimental J(T ) curves, measured in the absence of any saturation ﬁeld, especially in the case of hematite-bearing rocks [e.g., Duﬀ, 1979]. The theoretical substantiation of the peaks in the thermal magnetization and susceptibility curves observed for a great number of compounds was of- fered by I. Y. Korenblit and E. F. Sample MT95-1: Rhyolite Porphyry (Saugus) Rhyolite porphyry from Castle Hill, Saugus, Massachusetts (BOS18 in Fig. 1; analysis 3 in Table DR1, see footnote 1), represents a shallow intrusive or subvolcanic phase of the Lynn V ol- canic Complex. The porphyry contains albite phenocrysts in a granophyric groundmass of albite, K-feldspar, and interstitial quartz with accessory allanite, apatite, ilmenite, and zir- con. Four zircons, including three pretreated by chemical abrasion (z3, z5, and z6 in Table 1; see discussion of CA-TIMS in Appendix 1) and one pretreated by air abrasion (z4), yield overlap- ping analyses with a weighted mean 206Pb/238U date of 595.8 ± 1.2 Ma and an MSWD (mean square of weighted deviates) of 0.63 (Fig. 2A). Assuming that Pb loss is minimal or absent, this date is interpreted as the crystallization age of the rhyolite porphyry. Slightly younger Pb/U dates from air-abraded grains z8 and z9 prob- ably reﬂ ect Pb loss because air abrasion is gen- erally less effective than chemical abrasion in removing high U domains where Pb loss is most likely to occur. Sample MT-KK10: Rhyolitic Ash-Flow Tuff (Needham) Pyroclastic rhyolite from Needham, Mas- sachusetts (BOS 10 in Fig. 1), was collected from part of the Mattapan V olcanic Complex previously designated as the High Rock Tuff (analysis 7 in Thompson and Hermes, 1990). The dated sample consists of quartz, K-feld- spar, albite, and altered biotite phenocrysts stud- ded through a cryptocrystalline, felsitic matrix. Sparse pumice clasts are devitriﬁ ed to form irregular lenses of quartz and feldspar. Acces- sory minerals include apatite, magnetite, and zircon. Five out of six analyzed single zircons (z16, z17, z19, z20, z21 in Table 1 and Fig. 2C) yield a weighted mean 207Pb/206Pb date of 596.0 ± 1.4 Ma (MSWD = 0.78), which overlaps well within error with their upper concordia intercept date of 595.5 ± 0.8 Ma (MSWD = 0.17). This component is found in and around maﬁ c dikes at Worlds End (BOS15B, BOS15G, and BOS15J), where hematite staining is common on joints and fractures. We suspect that individual cores have locally intersected such surfaces, so that some of the BOS15G samples exhibit the C compo- nent and some A component. The mean direction calculated from the A component of magnetization at nine Lynn- Mattapan sites has a declination (D) of 319.9° and an inclination (I) of 57.0° ( α95 = 7.4°); the paleopole based on this mean direction is 206°E, 60°N. These results pass both rever- sals and fold tests and are regionally consis- tent among lithologies that include basalt, andesite, rhyodacite, and rhyolite, which rep- resent both volcanic and subvolcanic phases. Most sites also contain stable B and C mag- netic components with directions that suggest Ordovician to Permian remagnetizations. A broadly comparable A component direction with D = 109.0° and I = −63.4° (α95 = 9.4°, n = 11 samples) was obtained from one site in the Squantum Member of the Roxbury Con- glomerate (maximum age of 593 Ma) overly- ing the volcanic sequence. The Lynn-Mattapan results indicate that southeastern New England occupied a mid- latitude position at ca. 595 Ma, similar to those reported from Avalonian terranes in maritime Canada. The most likely peri- Gondwanan position for Avalonia consis- tent with these paleomagnetic data lies off the West African margin. Few structural corrections are required for these assessments, because Lynn and Mattapan volcanic rocks were generally protected against later deformation by their position directly above the massive Dedham Granite. Elsewhere, the volcanic rocks show no cleavage or any other textural evidence for tectonic deformation. In order to provide new constraints on them, a paleomagnetic study was carried out on the Ediacaran succession of red claystones exposed in Sierra de los Barrientos (37.8 ◦S, 59.0◦W), Buenos Aires province, Argentina. This succesion belongs to the late Proterozoic–early Paleozoic sedimentary cover of the Rio de la Plata craton. Sixty-two oriented samples from 13 sites were submitted to standard stepwise demagnetization procedures yielding a characteristic remanence carried by hematite. A primary origin for the remanence is suggested by the apparent recording of secular variation along the stratigraphic column including a reversal of the earth magnetic ﬁeld and an improvement in clustering of mean site directions after application of bedding corrections, although the latter is not statistically signiﬁcant. Since the study samples show a signiﬁcant anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) degree ( P up to 1.2) and an ellipsoid shape compatible with signiﬁcant compaction during diagenesis,

, in Northeast Brazil, and its African counterparts in Nigeria and Hoggar typify the tectonic evolution of the collisional belts encircling the São Francisco craton [13–15]. Never- theless, the margins of Kalahari, Rio de la Plata and Amazon cratons, as well as the southern border of the São Francisco craton, record much younger collision events, ageing up to Cambrian times ( Fig. 1 a). In spite of their similar ages all over South America, these Cambrian events are usually viewed as of local extent. They have been named Buzius Orogeny in southeast- ern Brazil [10], and Pampean Orogeny in western Argentina [16]. Paleomagnetism provides key information to con- strain such a complex assembly history. However, the scarcity of paleomagnetic data for late Neoproterozoic and Cambrian rocks in the West Gondwana has prevented testing these geodynamic scenarios (for a review, see [17]). Here we present a high-quality paleomagnetic pole obtained on the Early Cambrian mafic dikes of Itabaiana, Paraíba State, NE Brazil. These results are then compared with data from Gondwana, Laurentia and with poles recently obtained for the Amazon craton [18]. Introduction The assembly of Gondwana is now viewed as a long-standing protracted process that may encompass most of the Neoprotero- zoic era (e.g., Meert, 2003; Trindade et al., 2006; Vaughan and Pankhurst, 2008). However, reconstructing the paleogeography of this supercontinent in its early stages is a challenging prospect, so far impeded by the scarcity of relevant well-dated paleopoles in almost all cratonic units involved. The Congo craton, a central piece of the Gondwana jigsaw-puzzle, counts only 10 Proterozoic pale- opoles between 1300 and 550 Ma (Tohver et al., 2006). These poles mainly belong to two age groups: an older one (800–700 Ma) show- ing the rapid drift of Congo before the Panafrican orogenic events, and a younger one (550–500 Ma) corresponding to the time of ﬁnal assembly of Gondwana elements. With a growing body of information sup- porting periods of exceedingly unusual climate behavior for Earth in the Neoproterozoic, additional, robust pale- omagnetic data for this time period have become even more important. Some initial paleomagnetic data from mid-Neoproterozoic rocks from North America (e.g., Park and Aitken, 1986; Elston, 1993; Park et al., 1995; Weil et al., 2003, 2004) are consistent with the possibil- ity of North America lying at or near the equator during this time period, but some of these data sets are of limited quality and their overall reliability is open to question. To better understand the drift history and the APWP of Laurentia for the latest Neoproterozoic, we have under- taken a comprehensive paleomagnetic study of the Neo- proterozoic Uinta Mountain Group (UMG), northeast Utah, northwest Colorado, and southwest Wyoming. The UMG is one of the thickest and best preserved Neopro- terozoic sedimentary rock successions in North America. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. thin the UMG have been interpreted as dominantly ﬂuvial basin deposits with a source to the east and north ( Hansen, 1965; Sanderson, 1984; Sanderson and Wiley, 1986; Farmer and Ball, 1997) or a mixed ﬂuvial-marine environment ( Wallace and Crittenden, 1969; Wallace, 1972; Dehler et al., 2006). Detailed sedimentologic and stratigraphic stud- ies are warranted to resolve questions about depositional environments, paleogeography, and basin type. The UMG ranges in thickness from 4 km in the west to over 7 km in the east (Link et al., 1993). The western UMG is composed of quartzose and arkosic sandstone and interbedded mudstone, much of which is hematite- cemented. The eastern section consists of conglomerate, sandstone and mudstone, and most sandstone units in the east are hematite-cemented redbeds (Hansen, 1965). The UMG nonconformably overlies the Red Creek Quartzite and Owiyukuts Complex (∼1.7–∼2.7 Ga,Hansen, 1965; Sears et al., 1982 ). Methods Twelve sampling localities were established in UMG rocks. These include seven localities in the eastern Uintas (Home Mountain Canyon, Irish Canyon, Bull Canyon, Sparks, Lone Mountain, Cross Mountain, and Juniper Mountain) and, ﬁve localities in the north-central Uin- tas (Sheep Creek Canyon, Browne Lake, Carter Creek, Dowd Springs, and Flaming Gorge Reservoir dam) (Fig. 2). With a growing body of information sup- porting periods of exceedingly unusual climate behavior for Earth in the Neoproterozoic, additional, robust pale- omagnetic data for this time period have become even more important. Some initial paleomagnetic data from mid-Neoproterozoic rocks from North America (e.g., Park and Aitken, 1986; Elston, 1993; Park et al., 1995; Weil et al., 2003, 2004) are consistent with the possibil- ity of North America lying at or near the equator during this time period, but some of these data sets are of limited quality and their overall reliability is open to question. To better understand the drift history and the APWP of Laurentia for the latest Neoproterozoic, we have under- taken a comprehensive paleomagnetic study of the Neo- proterozoic Uinta Mountain Group (UMG), northeast Utah, northwest Colorado, and southwest Wyoming. The UMG is one of the thickest and best preserved Neopro- terozoic sedimentary rock successions in North America. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. thin the UMG have been interpreted as dominantly ﬂuvial basin deposits with a source to the east and north ( Hansen, 1965; Sanderson, 1984; Sanderson and Wiley, 1986; Farmer and Ball, 1997) or a mixed ﬂuvial-marine environment ( Wallace and Crittenden, 1969; Wallace, 1972; Dehler et al., 2006). Detailed sedimentologic and stratigraphic stud- ies are warranted to resolve questions about depositional environments, paleogeography, and basin type. The UMG ranges in thickness from 4 km in the west to over 7 km in the east (Link et al., 1993). The western UMG is composed of quartzose and arkosic sandstone and interbedded mudstone, much of which is hematite- cemented. The eastern section consists of conglomerate, sandstone and mudstone, and most sandstone units in the east are hematite-cemented redbeds (Hansen, 1965). The UMG nonconformably overlies the Red Creek Quartzite and Owiyukuts Complex (∼1.7–∼2.7 Ga,Hansen, 1965; Sears et al., 1982 ). Methods Twelve sampling localities were established in UMG rocks. These include seven localities in the eastern Uintas (Home Mountain Canyon, Irish Canyon, Bull Canyon, Sparks, Lone Mountain, Cross Mountain, and Juniper Mountain) and, ﬁve localities in the north-central Uin- tas (Sheep Creek Canyon, Browne Lake, Carter Creek, Dowd Springs, and Flaming Gorge Reservoir dam) (Fig. 2). The localities were selected based on exposure of continuous and thick sections of strata. Sampling was focused on hematite-cemented medium to ﬁne-grained sandstone and siltstone. With a growing body of information sup- porting periods of exceedingly unusual climate behavior for Earth in the Neoproterozoic, additional, robust pale- omagnetic data for this time period have become even more important. Some initial paleomagnetic data from mid-Neoproterozoic rocks from North America (e.g., Park and Aitken, 1986; Elston, 1993; Park et al., 1995; Weil et al., 2003, 2004) are consistent with the possibil- ity of North America lying at or near the equator during this time period, but some of these data sets are of limited quality and their overall reliability is open to question. To better understand the drift history and the APWP of Laurentia for the latest Neoproterozoic, we have under- taken a comprehensive paleomagnetic study of the Neo- proterozoic Uinta Mountain Group (UMG), northeast Utah, northwest Colorado, and southwest Wyoming. The UMG is one of the thickest and best preserved Neopro- terozoic sedimentary rock successions in North America. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acqui- sition and backﬁeld demagnetization experiments, using a pulse DC magnet capable of ﬁelds of 3.2 T, were per- formed on selected samples from all localities to further evaluate the magnetic mineralogy. Three-axis IRM ther- mal demagnetization experiments ( Lowrie, 1990) were performed using three DC ﬁelds (3.0, 0.3, and 0.03 T; or “hard,” “medium” and “soft,” respectively) along three orthogonal axes. Remanence directions were calculated from princi- pal component analysis ( Kirschvink, 1980 ) of linear vectors picked from orthogonal projection demagneti- zation plots (Zijderveld, 1967). Estimated directions for specimens were accepted for site mean determinations if unanchored maximum angular deviation (MAD) val- ues were less than 15 ◦. Specimens that could not be resolved to MADs of less than 15 ◦, as well as those specimens with anomalous directions (i.e., individual direction greater than two angular standard deviations from the estimated mean) were rejected for site mean calculations. thin the UMG have been interpreted as dominantly ﬂuvial basin deposits with a source to the east and north ( Hansen, 1965; Sanderson, 1984; Sanderson and Wiley, 1986; Farmer and Ball, 1997) or a mixed ﬂuvial-marine environment ( Wallace and Crittenden, 1969; Wallace, 1972; Dehler et al., 2006). Detailed sedimentologic and stratigraphic stud- ies are warranted to resolve questions about depositional environments, paleogeography, and basin type. The UMG ranges in thickness from 4 km in the west to over 7 km in the east (Link et al., 1993). The western UMG is composed of quartzose and arkosic sandstone and interbedded mudstone, much of which is hematite- cemented. The eastern section consists of conglomerate, sandstone and mudstone, and most sandstone units in the east are hematite-cemented redbeds (Hansen, 1965). The UMG nonconformably overlies the Red Creek Quartzite and Owiyukuts Complex (∼1.7–∼2.7 Ga,Hansen, 1965; Sears et al., 1982 ). The Red Creek Quartzite and Owiyukuts Complex are composed of metaquartzite, amphibolite and mica schist ( Schell, 1969; Sears et al., 1982; Hansen, 1984 ) and are restricted to the struc- turally high, northeastern region of the Uinta Mountains. Rock magnetism and magnetic mineralogy, UMG Rocks Thermal demagnetization of all UMG rocks inves- tigated reveals that hematite is the primary carrier of what we interpret as an ancient, primary to near primary Neoproterozoic magnetization as well as the secondary magnetization that is pervasive at many UMG localities. High laboratory unblocking temperatures were observed for almost all of the samples, with most unblocking between about 600 ◦ and 670 ◦C. However, NRM intensi- ties show less of a correlation with the presence of a speciﬁc magnetization. In general, histograms of NRM intensities for specimens dominated by a secondary mag- netization show median values that are up to an order of magnitude greater than those of specimens that contain only the east or west-directed and shallow magnetiza- tion. Chemical demagnetization of NRM (Figs. 3b and c and 4b–f) shows that ﬁne-grained, pigmentary hematite is the principal form of hematite present in all UMG rocks. With a growing body of information sup- porting periods of exceedingly unusual climate behavior for Earth in the Neoproterozoic, additional, robust pale- omagnetic data for this time period have become even more important. Some initial paleomagnetic data from mid-Neoproterozoic rocks from North America (e.g., Park and Aitken, 1986; Elston, 1993; Park et al., 1995; Weil et al., 2003, 2004) are consistent with the possibil- ity of North America lying at or near the equator during this time period, but some of these data sets are of limited quality and their overall reliability is open to question. To better understand the drift history and the APWP of Laurentia for the latest Neoproterozoic, we have under- taken a comprehensive paleomagnetic study of the Neo- proterozoic Uinta Mountain Group (UMG), northeast Utah, northwest Colorado, and southwest Wyoming. The UMG is one of the thickest and best preserved Neopro- terozoic sedimentary rock successions in North America. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. Sampling was focused on hematite-cemented medium to ﬁne-grained sandstone and siltstone. Each site was deﬁned by an individual stratigraphic bed, or several successive beds, and 7–12 independently oriented samples were obtained. A total of 195 sites from 12 localities were collected in UMG strata. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) data were obtained using superconducting rock magnetometers in magnetically shielded rooms at the University of New Mexico and at the University of Michigan. Stepwise demagnetization was performed to determine the direc- tion of characteristic remanent magnetizations (ChRM). For all UMG rocks, both thermal and chemical demag- netization, using reagent grade hydrochloric acid at room temperature ( Henry, 1979), were used to effec- tively isolate ChRMs. Chemical demagnetization was performed in a low ﬁeld space ( H ∼200 nT) in a fume hood. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acqui- sition and backﬁeld demagnetization experiments, using a pulse DC magnet capable of ﬁelds of 3.2 T, were per- formed on selected samples from all localities to further evaluate the magnetic mineralogy. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acqui- sition and backﬁeld demagnetization experiments, using a pulse DC magnet capable of ﬁelds of 3.2 T, were per- formed on selected samples from all localities to further evaluate the magnetic mineralogy. Three-axis IRM ther- mal demagnetization experiments ( Lowrie, 1990) were performed using three DC ﬁelds (3.0, 0.3, and 0.03 T; or “hard,” “medium” and “soft,” respectively) along three orthogonal axes. Remanence directions were calculated from princi- pal component analysis ( Kirschvink, 1980 ) of linear vectors picked from orthogonal projection demagneti- zation plots (Zijderveld, 1967). Estimated directions for specimens were accepted for site mean determinations if unanchored maximum angular deviation (MAD) val- ues were less than 15 ◦. Specimens that could not be resolved to MADs of less than 15 ◦, as well as those specimens with anomalous directions (i.e., individual direction greater than two angular standard deviations from the estimated mean) were rejected for site mean calculations. With a growing body of information sup- porting periods of exceedingly unusual climate behavior for Earth in the Neoproterozoic, additional, robust pale- omagnetic data for this time period have become even more important. Some initial paleomagnetic data from mid-Neoproterozoic rocks from North America (e.g., Park and Aitken, 1986; Elston, 1993; Park et al., 1995; Weil et al., 2003, 2004) are consistent with the possibil- ity of North America lying at or near the equator during this time period, but some of these data sets are of limited quality and their overall reliability is open to question. To better understand the drift history and the APWP of Laurentia for the latest Neoproterozoic, we have under- taken a comprehensive paleomagnetic study of the Neo- proterozoic Uinta Mountain Group (UMG), northeast Utah, northwest Colorado, and southwest Wyoming. The UMG is one of the thickest and best preserved Neopro- terozoic sedimentary rock successions in North America. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. Evidence for such a remagnetiza- tion is compelling along the Mammoth fault in the northern Tobacco Root Mountains where a Laramide thrust fault intensely sheared and fractured the Mammoth diabase dike (Fig. 2B). The fault controlled the emplacement of the Tobacco Root Batholith (Schmidt et al., 1990 ) and acted as a conduit for late stage magmatic ﬂuids or ﬂuids associated with subsequent precious mineralization. Evidence for ﬂuid activity includes extensive chloritization and epidotization of the dike, and locally intense siliciﬁcation. The remanence may have been caused by growth of secondary magnetite around original titanomagnetite grains, by growth of new magnetite by precipitation of iron during for- mation of secondary alteration phases, or by a combination of both processes. e ﬁne- to medium-grained ( ≤1 to 2 mm average grain size) diabase. They consist of clinopyroxene (augite) and plagioclase, with minor biotite and amphibole. These dikes are ophitic and subophitic to intergranular; porphyritic and glom- eroporphyritic textures are sometimes present. Group A dikes are thin, with thicknesses ranging from 2 to 7 m. Evidence for such a remagnetiza- tion is compelling along the Mammoth fault in the northern Tobacco Root Mountains where a Laramide thrust fault intensely sheared and fractured the Mammoth diabase dike (Fig. 2B). The fault controlled the emplacement of the Tobacco Root Batholith (Schmidt et al., 1990 ) and acted as a conduit for late stage magmatic ﬂuids or ﬂuids associated with subsequent precious mineralization. Evidence for ﬂuid activity includes extensive chloritization and epidotization of the dike, and locally intense siliciﬁcation. The remanence may have been caused by growth of secondary magnetite around original titanomagnetite grains, by growth of new magnetite by precipitation of iron during for- mation of secondary alteration phases, or by a combination of both processes. Some magnetite may also have formed during oxidation of magmatic sulﬁdes present within the dike. It is unlikely to be the result of widespread tectonothermal activity with temperatures greater than 300 ◦C given the preservation of Proterozoic ages from biotites in basement rocks from the southern Tobacco Root Mountains, including the biotite from the baked contact zone at site TR50 described above. Evidence for such a remagnetiza- tion is compelling along the Mammoth fault in the northern Tobacco Root Mountains where a Laramide thrust fault intensely sheared and fractured the Mammoth diabase dike (Fig. 2B). The fault controlled the emplacement of the Tobacco Root Batholith (Schmidt et al., 1990 ) and acted as a conduit for late stage magmatic ﬂuids or ﬂuids associated with subsequent precious mineralization. Evidence for ﬂuid activity includes extensive chloritization and epidotization of the dike, and locally intense siliciﬁcation. The remanence may have been caused by growth of secondary magnetite around original titanomagnetite grains, by growth of new magnetite by precipitation of iron during for- mation of secondary alteration phases, or by a combination of both processes. Some magnetite may also have formed during oxidation of magmatic sulﬁdes present within the dike. New paleomagnetic and 40Ar–39Ar geochronologic results have been obtained from a pair of shallowly emplaced syenitic intrusions in western Quebec. Horn- blende grains at site CG13 of the Chatham-Grenville stock either do not yield a stable plateau or appear to be compromised by the degassing of pyroxene with the hornblende, thus leading us to exclude site 13 from the overall age estimate. The remaining three sample sites MR10, CG31 and CG14 ( Fig. 2 ) provide an overall hornblende 40Ar–39Ar age of 531.9± 1.4 Ma (weighted mean of the ﬁve hornblende plateau ages). The potassium feldspar age data from all four sam- ple sites record 39Ar loss at some point in their history; all analysed potassium feldspars exhibit an apparent age minima at ∼5–25% degassed 39Ar, followed by a “stair- case” degassing spectrum of increasing apparent age. The feldspars B86a and B86b from site CG31 ( Fig. 3e) may be considered the least disturbed of those analysed, having the least prominent minimum apparent age (of ca. 460 Ma) and latter step ages that approach the horn- blende age from the site, as well as total gas ages of ca. 535 Ma. Overall, the potassium feldspars from the two stocks are most simply interpreted as having initially closed in the early Paleozoic, if not in the Early Cam- brian itself, with a subsequent reheating event having caused variable 39Ar loss. Laurentia likely resided at low southerly paleolatitudes throughout the Cambrian, ruling out a major inertial-interchange TPW event for Early to Middle Cambrian time. A comparison of Late Ediacaran to Middle Cambrian paleomagnetic results from Laurentia, Baltica, Siberia and elements of West Gondwana implies that by Early Cambrian time a large paleolatitudinal gap existed between Laurentia and its presumed conjugate rift margins, thus placing a wide Iapetus Ocean between them. The position of Baltica within the circum-Iapetus paleogeography is contentious, due to differing interpretations of the few paleomagnetic results. During Ediacaran time, Laurentia underwent large apparent polar wander that is manifested as motion from low latitude at 615 Ma to the south polar region at 590–575 Ma, and then rapidly back to low latitude by 565–550 Ma. These rapid apparent motions complicate attempts to reconstruct the paleogeography, and have led to non-uniformitarian proposals such as rapid plate motion during the terminal Neoproterozoic opening of the Iapetus (McCausland and Hodych, 1998; Cawood et al., 2001 ) or the contribution of substantial true polar wander (TPW) during the Early Cambrian (Kirschvink et al., 1997; Evans, 1998). This study provides new hornblende and potassium feldspar 40Ar–39Ar age dating and primary paleomag- netic results for the Mont Rigaud and Chatham-Grenville stocks of western Quebec. The paleomagnetic results apply to Laurentia for Early Cambrian time, a period which is not well represented for Laurentia. The 40Ar–39Ar ages also extend the region of recognized Early Cambrian rift-related magmatism of Laurentia’s Iapetan margin to include the northeastern Laurentia, conﬁrming that rift-related activity took place there for ca. 80 myears during Ediacaran to Early Cambrian time. 2. Paleomagnetism The Mont Rigaud and Chatham-Grenville stocks were sampled by portable gas-powered drill and as ori- ented hand-samples. Both methods produced standard 2.54 cm diameter core samples, and each paleomagnetic site consisted typically of six samples. The Mont Rigaud stock and environs were sampled in 27 sites, providing 320 standard 2.2 cm length specimens for analysis and the Chatham-Grenville stock and environs were sampled in 31 sites, providing 305 specimens. The specimens underwent thermal and alternating ﬁeld (AF) stepwise demagnetization at the University of Michigan using a Sapphire Instruments SI-4 AF demag- netizer, an ASC TD-48 thermal demagnetizer, and a 2G cryogenic magnetometer, all set inside a magnetically shielded room which permits entry of only∼0.2% of the Earth’s ambient magnetic ﬁeld intensity. A subset of 62 specimens from Mont Rigaud were thermally and AF demagnetized at the University of Windsor paleomag- netics laboratory using similar equipment in a similar low ambient magnetic ﬁeld environment. Hand-picked separates of horn- blende and potassium feldspar grains were rinsed with deionized water and dried. Single, non-aggregate grains of 1–2 mm size were then selected under a binocular microscope for further analysis. Several grains from each site were packaged at the University of Michigan Radio- genic Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory in an aluminum foil capsule and irradiated for 300 h at the Phoenix-Ford Memorial Reactor at the University of Michigan. Neu- tron ﬂux gradients were monitored using the MMhb-1 standard (520.4 Ma; Samson and Alexander, 1987). During analysis, single grains were step-heated until fusion by an automated argon-ion laser which was defocused to ensure uniform heating. Individual steps consisted of 60 s heating followed by 2 min of gas puriﬁ- cation using two 10 1/s SAES getters (ST101 alloy) and a liquid N 2 cold ﬁnger to remove the active gasses prior to mass spectrometry. Argon isotopic ratios were measured with a VG1200S mass spectrometer. Extraction line blanks were run after every six steps. Horn- blende grains at site CG13 of the Chatham-Grenville stock either do not yield a stable plateau or appear to be compromised by the degassing of pyroxene with the hornblende, thus leading us to exclude site 13 from the overall age estimate. The remaining three sample sites MR10, CG31 and CG14 ( Fig. 2 ) provide an overall hornblende 40Ar–39Ar age of 531.9± 1.4 Ma (weighted mean of the ﬁve hornblende plateau ages). The potassium feldspar age data from all four sam- ple sites record 39Ar loss at some point in their history; all analysed potassium feldspars exhibit an apparent age minima at ∼5–25% degassed 39Ar, followed by a “stair- case” degassing spectrum of increasing apparent age. The feldspars B86a and B86b from site CG31 ( Fig. 3e) may be considered the least disturbed of those analysed, having the least prominent minimum apparent age (of ca. 460 Ma) and latter step ages that approach the horn- blende age from the site, as well as total gas ages of ca. 535 Ma. Overall, the potassium feldspars from the two stocks are most simply interpreted as having initially closed in the early Paleozoic, if not in the Early Cam- brian itself, with a subsequent reheating event having caused variable 39Ar loss. A comparison of Late Ediacaran to Middle Cambrian paleomagnetic results from Laurentia, Baltica, Siberia and elements of West Gondwana implies that by Early Cambrian time a large paleolatitudinal gap existed between Laurentia and its presumed conjugate rift margins, thus placing a wide Iapetus Ocean between them. The position of Baltica within the circum-Iapetus paleogeography is contentious, due to differing interpretations of the few paleomagnetic results. During Ediacaran time, Laurentia underwent large apparent polar wander that is manifested as motion from low latitude at 615 Ma to the south polar region at 590–575 Ma, and then rapidly back to low latitude by 565–550 Ma. These rapid apparent motions complicate attempts to reconstruct the paleogeography, and have led to non-uniformitarian proposals such as rapid plate motion during the terminal Neoproterozoic opening of the Iapetus (McCausland and Hodych, 1998; Cawood et al., 2001 ) or the contribution of substantial true polar wander (TPW) during the Early Cambrian (Kirschvink et al., 1997; Evans, 1998). This study provides new hornblende and potassium feldspar 40Ar–39Ar age dating and primary paleomag- netic results for the Mont Rigaud and Chatham-Grenville stocks of western Quebec. The paleomagnetic results apply to Laurentia for Early Cambrian time, a period which is not well represented for Laurentia. The 40Ar–39Ar ages also extend the region of recognized Early Cambrian rift-related magmatism of Laurentia’s Iapetan margin to include the northeastern Laurentia, conﬁrming that rift-related activity took place there for ca. 80 myears during Ediacaran to Early Cambrian time. 2. Paleomagnetism The Mont Rigaud and Chatham-Grenville stocks were sampled by portable gas-powered drill and as ori- ented hand-samples. Both methods produced standard 2.54 cm diameter core samples, and each paleomagnetic site consisted typically of six samples. The Mont Rigaud stock and environs were sampled in 27 sites, providing 320 standard 2.2 cm length specimens for analysis and the Chatham-Grenville stock and environs were sampled in 31 sites, providing 305 specimens. The specimens underwent thermal and alternating ﬁeld (AF) stepwise demagnetization at the University of Michigan using a Sapphire Instruments SI-4 AF demag- netizer, an ASC TD-48 thermal demagnetizer, and a 2G cryogenic magnetometer, all set inside a magnetically shielded room which permits entry of only∼0.2% of the Earth’s ambient magnetic ﬁeld intensity. A subset of 62 specimens from Mont Rigaud were thermally and AF demagnetized at the University of Windsor paleomag- netics laboratory using similar equipment in a similar low ambient magnetic ﬁeld environment. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: owball Earth hypothesis, paleomagnetic investigations were carried out in the Aksu area of the northwestern Tarim basin. Forty-eight sites of samples were collected from the Sugetbrak and Chigebrak Formations. Twenty-four sites of sandstone and volcanic rock from the Sugetbrak Formation revealed stable characteristic remanent components (ChRm) isolated between 500 and 680 ◦C. The computed magnetic directions from these components are consistent and signiﬁcantly distinguished from those of younger ages. Both normal and reverse polarities have been observed, and a positive fold test is revealed after bedding corrections at 95% conﬁdence level. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility measurements shows primary sedimentary fabrics with weak anisotropy degrees. It is mainly a porphyritic to coarse-grained equigranular monzogranite, with crystallization age of ∼ 370 and cooling age of ∼ 340 Ma, presently exposed as asymmetric, eastward-tilted blocks. Forty-three sites were sampled in the Achala monzogranite. Overall, it is weakly magnetic, with a mean magnetic susceptibility of 15 × 10 − 5 (SI). Twenty-two sites showed unstable magnetic behaviour. The remaining 21 sites have haematite as magnetic carrier of a stable remanence. The ilmeno-haematite appears as an accessory mineral, with exsolved intergrowths of (haemo)ilmenite. Thermal demagnetisation up to 620 –640 °C isolated steeply-dipping, dual-polarity remanence directions. The palaeomagnetic pole is located at 56°S, 307°E ( N = 18, A95 10.7, K 11). The remanence was locked on cooling, over a range of temperatures from magnetic ordering to exsolution of ilmenite –haematite ( ∼600 to 390 °C). The pole better coincides with the 370 – 360 Ma segment of the Gondwana apparent polar wander path, suggesting that remanence was acquired quickly. Introduction From its assemblage at around 550 Ma to its amalgamation with Laurussia to form Pangaea in the latest Palaeozoic, the Gondwana supercontinent seems to have wandered over the South Pole following a complex path, as suggested by the palaeomagnetic poles determined from its main constituent plates, especially Australia, Africa and South America. Many versions of the apparent polar wander path (APWP) proposed for Gondwana (e.g. Morel and Irving, 1978; Kent and V an der V oo, 1990; Chen et al., 1993; McElhinny et al., 2003 ) share in common the fact of being constituted by several long segments separated by sharp hairpins. Plate reorganization events, true polar wander episodes, and high plate velocities, have been interpreted on the basis of the length of the APWP segments and the timing of the hairpins (e.g. Meert et al., 1993; V an der V oo, 1993; McElhinny et al., 2003; Evans, 2003; Piper, 2007 ). The complexities of the Palaeozoic APWP include a Silurian–Devonian segment defining a loop passing by southern South America. This loop, mainly based on palaeomagnetic poles from eastern Australia, has been questioned by some authors, as it implies a very high drift rate for Gondwana. The complexities of the Palaeozoic APWP include a Silurian–Devonian segment defining a loop passing by southern South America. Introduction From its assemblage at around 550 Ma to its amalgamation with Laurussia to form Pangaea in the latest Palaeozoic, the Gondwana supercontinent seems to have wandered over the South Pole following a complex path, as suggested by the palaeomagnetic poles determined from its main constituent plates, especially Australia, Africa and South America. Many versions of the apparent polar wander path (APWP) proposed for Gondwana (e.g. Morel and Irving, 1978; Kent and V an der V oo, 1990; Chen et al., 1993; McElhinny et al., 2003 ) share in common the fact of being constituted by several long segments separated by sharp hairpins. Plate reorganization events, true polar wander episodes, and high plate velocities, have been interpreted on the basis of the length of the APWP segments and the timing of the hairpins (e.g. Meert et al., 1993; V an der V oo, 1993; McElhinny et al., 2003; Evans, 2003; Piper, 2007 ). The complexities of the Palaeozoic APWP include a Silurian–Devonian segment defining a loop passing by southern South America.

Baltica in Columbia The paleogeography of Baltica is based on the mean of two key poles: the 1770 Ma Ropruchey Sills and the ca. 1790 Ma Shosksha Formation. The ﬁrst one is obtained from well-dated 1770± 12 Ma (U–Pb) gabbros and dolerites from the Ropruchey Sills whose mag- netizatizion is considered primary in origin (Fedotova et al., 1999). The second one is determined from sandstones from the top of the Shosksha Formation ( Pisarevsky and Sokolov, 2001 ). These sedi

c Province (THO) suggest high paleolatitudes for Laurentia, whereas poles from cratonic provinces (Superior, Churchill and Coronation) indicate moderate paleolatitudes. The 1830 Ma Molson dikes (Superior Craton) yield three components but the primary or secondary nature of these components is debatable ( Zhai et al., 1994; Halls and Heaman, 2000 ). The Peninsular sills (Coro- nation Province) yield well-clustered low-inclination remanence directions (Irving and McGlynn, 1979), and the calculated pole has been used by Pesonen et al. (2003) for a 1770 Ma reconstruction. However, this pole cannot be considered a key pole due to its inconclusive baked contact test and the poor age constraints (a Rb–Sr isochron age of 1800 Ma). Park et al. (1973) obtained pale- omagnetic data for sedimentary rocks of the Kazan Formation, volcanic rocks from Christopher Island Formation (Dubawnt Group- Churchill province) besides two large dikes considered as feeding dikes of the Christopher Island lava ﬂows. All these rocks presented consistent results that passed reversal and baked contact tests. K–Ar dating in biotite and phlogopite of the igneous rocks yielded a mean age of 1716 Ma, but more recent studies attribute an older age, between 1830 and 1760 Ma, for the Dubawnt Group (Rainbird and Hadlari, 2000). Received 2006 August 4; in original form 2006 April 1 SUMMARY The pole position for the late Mesoproterozoic Alcurra (formerly Kulgera) Dyke Swarm (ADS), Musgrave Block, central Australia, has been revised by adding new data from two more dykes. A palaeomagnetic fold test is positive at the 99 percent conﬁdence level and the pole position is latitude = 2.8 ◦ S, longitude= 80.4◦E( dp = 7.2◦, dm = 10.7◦). on two samples of aggregates of very ﬁne-grained biotite from the mesostasis of a Stuart Dyke (SD), Arunta Inlier, Northern Territory, yield ages of 1059± 2 and 1066 ± 3M a( 2σ ). These new ages are in agreement with those of the ∼1070 Ma Warakurna large igneous province, west-central Australia, indicating that both the ADS and SD belong to that suite. Palaeomagnetic poles determined by others for the ADS and SD are indistinguishable from each other but cannot be presently combined as a single pole because the published information on the SD is incomplete. An analysis of the palaeogeography implied by the dispersed palaeomagnetic poles from members of the extended Warakurna suite shows that the present relationships between the major Precambrian cratons (West, North and South Australian), which constitute Australia west of the Tasman Line, are inconsistent with the inferred relationship at∼1070 Ma. Nor is it apparent that internal deformations within the separate cratons are the cause of the dispersion. Our ﬁndings imply that these major Australian Cratons must have ﬁnally assembled sometime after ∼1070 Ma. Anisotropy of Magnetic Susceptibility (AMS) and Structural Control [13] Bedding control is one of the major difficulties in these massive volcanic rocks. Measurements of the AMS indicate the preferred orientation of magnetic minerals, and are used here in two ways. On the one hand, it is one of the best tools to evaluate the degree of internal strain in rocks and is necessary to discard the possibility of deviations of the natural remanent magnetization [e.g., Tarling and Hrouda, 1993; Cogne´, 1987]. On the other hand, the shape and orientation of the ellipsoid of magnetic susceptibility can be regarded as an independent ind

ineation cannot correspond to the magmatic flow, as these rocks are part of a subhorizontal lava flow (K. Bull, written communication, 2003). The possibility that this vertical elongation results from horizon- tal contraction associated with the formation of jointing can also be discounted, since magnetite or a magnetite-like mineral, which probably predominantly controlled the sus- ceptibility (see rock magnetism, below), is crystallized at much higher temperature than the temperature at which columnar jointing forms. The vertical elongation must then correspond to tectonic effects. Although horizontal K min usually indicates strong strain, AMS parameters show that this is not the case here as the degree of anisotropy is only about 5%. [ 17] The most plausible explanation for the vertical K max is that the ellipsoid of magnetic susceptibility was nearly a sphere, with no original compaction magnetic fabric to overcome. A paleomagnetic study was carried out in the well-dated Ambone and Ural volcanics in the central subprovince of Lachlan Orogen, New South Wales. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility measurements confirms detailed mapping of the region and shows that these massive dacitic sills and/or lava flows are flat lying. Among the different localities studied, only one yields interpretable paleomagnetic results. Two components of magnetization can be identified: a midtemperature direction yielding a corresponding pole in Australian coordinates l = 67.9 S/ f = 084.4 E (B = 5; n = 21; dp = 17.5 /dm = 23.1 ) and a high- temperature direction with a corresponding VGPl = 24.4 S/f = 060.6 E (B = 5; n = 25; dp = 1.4 /dm = 2.5 ). The first is interpreted as corresponding to an Early Carboniferous pole position and can be regarded as an overprint probably related to the Early Carboniferous Kanimblan orogenic event. The second does not correspond to any expected Silurian- Devonian or younger pole position. This magnetization is thought to be primary in orig

and Morel and Irving [1978] for an alternative model). In such a situation, the use of paleomagnetic data from Lachlan Orogen should not be used to define the APW path of Gondwana. As part of a project on the Gondwana APW path, this paper reports findings of a paleomagnetic study of rift basins in the central subprovince of the Lachlan Orogen (New South Wales) that has implications for both global paleogeography and the tectonic evolution of the orogen (Figure 2). 2. Geological Setting [5] The Lachlan Orogen is divided into several structural subprovinces, three in the models of Gray et al. [1997] and four in the models of Glen [1992, 2005]. Samples described in this paper are located in the central subprovince of the Lachlan Orogen, lying inboard (west) of relics of former intraoceanic island arc, the Macquarie V olcanic Arc (Figure 2) that formed from west dipping subduction, throughout the Ordovician [ Glen et al. , 1998, 2003; Glen, 2004; Glen et al. , 2004]. [ 6] After the Late Ordovician – Early Silurian Benambran Orogeny in which Ordovician craton-derived turbidite ter- ranes were assembled adjacent to the arc [ Glen, 2005], the plate boundary between the proto-Pacific plate and the Gondwana margin underwent major rollback back to the east. As a result, the Silurian – Middle Dev

former intraoceanic island arc, the Macquarie V olcanic Arc (Figure 2) that formed from west dipping subduction, throughout the Ordovician [ Glen et al. , 1998, 2003; Glen, 2004; Glen et al. , 2004]. [ 6] After the Late Ordovician – Early Silurian Benambran Orogeny in which Ordovician craton-derived turbidite ter- ranes were assembled adjacent to the arc [ Glen, 2005], the plate boundary between the proto-Pacific plate and the Gondwana margin underwent major rollback back to the east. As a result, the Silurian – Middle Devonian history of the Lachlan Orogen is marked by extension in a back arc position. This Tabberabberan cycle was marked by formation of rift basins and emplacement of granitic bodies [ Glen, 2004, 2005]. Major Late Silurian – Early Devonian rift basins in the central subprovince of the Lachlan Orogen include the Cobar Basin, the Mount Hope Trough and the Rast Trough [Glen et al. , 1996], which were separated or flanked by shallow water shelves: the Winduck, Walters Range and Kopyje shelves (Figure 2). Overlying these were late Early to Late Devonian fluviatile strata of the Mulga Downs and Cocoparra groups [Colquhoun et al., 2000]. The Mount Hope Trough [Scheibner, 1987] is filled by volcanics and volcani- clastic rocks of the poorly dated Late Silurian to Early Devonian

2000]. The Mount Hope Trough [Scheibner, 1987] is filled by volcanics and volcani- clastic rocks of the poorly dated Late Silurian to Early Devonian Mount Hope Group that interfingers at the top with siliciclastic turbidites of the Broken Range Group [Scheibner, 1987]. One major unit, the Ambone V olcanics, consists of two massive lava flows separated by partly turbiditic sediments. Lava units show well-developed columnar jointing. These rocks are rhyodacite porphyries, and are thought to have been extruded as extensive submarine lava flows in the latest Pragian [ Scheibner, 1987]. They were deformed in the late Early – Middle Devonian with formation of north- south folds with wavelengths of km. Late Devonian strata to the west and south of the region were folded into open broad folds in the Carboniferous [ Scheibner, 1987; Glen et al. , 1996]. These lava flows were sampled over several hundreds of meters of section close to the Mount Hope township (termed locality ‘‘HOP’’). The sampled locality was on the eastern limb of a 1-km-wide syncline occupied by Ambone V olcanics. The western limb of the structure is cleaved and sheared and was not sampled. These uncertainties are due to the lack of reliable paleomagnetic data from the Gondwana continents for this key period, leading to different Apparent Polar Wander Paths (APWP) for this supercontinent (e.g. Morel and Irving, 1978; Schmidt et al., 1990; Bachtadse and Briden, 1990; V an der V oo, 1993; McElhinny et al., 2003). The African APWP for the Paleozoic times is not very well defined, especially for the Upper Devonian – Lower Carboniferous (Bachtadse et al., 1987; Aifa et al., 1990; Bachtadse and Briden, 1991; Smith et al., 1994 ). Several paleomagnetic studies carried out on Devonian and Carboniferous sedimentary rocks in the stable Saharan craton (southern Algeria) in order to improve this curve, but the results correspond rather to secondary magnetizations ( Aifa, 1993; Derder et al., 1997; Bayou et al., 2000; Henry et al., 2004a ). Because magmatic rocks often present more accurate magnetic characteristics than those obtained from sedimentary rocks, paleomagnetic investigation was carried out on doleritic rocks. The dolerites subject to this study intruded the horizontal tabular Devonian formations of the Tin Serririne basin during Lower Carboniferous times. 2. The dolerites subject to this study intruded the horizontal tabular Devonian formations of the Tin Serririne basin during Lower Carboniferous times. 2. Geological setting The Hoggar shield, also called “Ahaggar”, consists of mesozonal to catazonal series of Archean, Eburnean and Neoproterozoic lithologies that are later intruded by granitic rocks. The Tin Serririne –Tin Mersoï basin is located on the south border of the Hoggar shield and extends southeasterly covering the northern part of Niger ( Fig. 1 ). It is composed of Paleozoic series that overly the Proterozoic basement of the Hoggar shield.
